nameStory: Planotaenium interruptum gets its scientific name from Latin words meaning "flat ribbon" and "interrupted," referring to its flattened, ribbon-like shape that appears to have breaks or gaps along its length. Since this microscopic algae lacks a widely-used common name, scientists stick with the descriptive Latin that captures its most distinctive feature - looking like a tiny, interrupted green ribbon under the microscope.
description: Planotaenium interruptum is a microscopic freshwater green algae that you'll never see with the naked eye - it requires a microscope to observe properly. This tiny organism appears as a flattened, ribbon-like cell that looks somewhat segmented or interrupted along its length, giving it its scientific name. Individual cells are extremely small, measuring only about 10-30 micrometers wide (that's smaller than the width of a human hair!). While invisible to us without magnification, these algae can form part of the greenish film or scum you might notice on the surface of quiet ponds and slow streams.

idTips.label: Ribbon-like shape
idTips.description: Under a microscope, cells appear as flattened ribbons with constricted areas that create an interrupted or segmented appearance along their length

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Cells show a bright green color due to chloroplasts, similar to other green algae, with the green pigment distributed throughout the flattened cell

idTips.label: Single-celled structure
idTips.description: Each organism consists of just one elongated, flattened cell rather than being made up of multiple connected cells

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Completely invisible to the naked eye, requiring at least 100x magnification to observe the characteristic shape and features

idTips.label: Aquatic habitat
idTips.description: Found floating in freshwater or as part of greenish films on water surfaces in ponds, slow streams, and wetlands

habitat: This microscopic algae lives in quiet freshwater environments throughout New England, including slow-moving streams, ponds, marshes, and wetland areas. Look for it in areas with still or gently flowing water where other green algae create visible films or scums on the surface. It prefers nutrient-rich waters and can be found from lowland areas up to moderate elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as waters warm and daylight increases. Best time to collect samples for microscopic observation as spring runoff brings fresh nutrients to water bodies.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when populations are most abundant. Warmer temperatures and longer days promote rapid reproduction, making this the ideal time for observation.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist into early fall but begin declining as temperatures drop and daylight decreases. Still observable but less abundant than summer months.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or present in very low numbers during the coldest months. Some cells may survive in ice-free areas but are difficult to locate for observation.

funFact: Despite being invisible to our eyes, Planotaenium interruptum and its microscopic relatives produce a significant portion of the oxygen we breathe - these tiny green ribbons are actually miniature oxygen factories floating in our ponds and streams!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it could be confused with other ribbon-like algae, but the characteristic constricted or interrupted appearance along its length is the key distinguishing feature. Remember: "interrupted ribbon" - if it looks like a smooth, unbroken ribbon, it's probably a different species.
contextualKnowledge: This organism represents one of the many microscopic life forms that most people never realize exist in every drop of pond water. While we focus on trees, flowers, and birds, an entire invisible world of algae, protists, and other microorganisms thrives all around us, playing crucial roles in aquatic ecosystems.
compareHints: Since Planotaenium interruptum appears to be the only member of its genus in New England waters, compare it with other ribbon-like freshwater algae in related families. Unlike the spiral-shaped cells of Spirogyra or the star-shaped colonies of other green algae, Planotaenium maintains its distinctive flattened, interrupted ribbon appearance. The key difference from similar microscopic algae is that segmented or constricted look that gives it the "interrupted" part of its name.
